vignette:
He is 29, European, and works in the Coast Guard, a job that once gave him a steady sense of competence. Before the robbery, he likes the discipline of it: the early starts, the drills, the clarity of procedure, the feeling that if something goes wrong there is a protocol to follow. He lives with his girlfriend in a small apartment near the harbor, and their routines are ordinary and reassuring. He runs on his days off, cooks simple meals, complains about weather reports, and checks locks almost absentmindedly, the way many people do before bed.

The robbery happens on an evening that begins without significance. He has finished a late shift and stops at a convenience store on the walk back from the station. He is tired, still half in work mode, thinking about a colleague's mistake during training and what he needs to bring in the next morning. As he cuts through a side street, he hears footsteps behind him but does not turn at first. When he does, there are two men close already. One grabs his jacket, the other demands his wallet and phone. He remembers the smell of cigarette smoke and wet pavement more clearly than their faces. He tries to hand over what they want quickly, but one of them shoves him hard against a wall and strikes him when he does not move fast enough. For a few seconds he is certain they are going to kill him. The thought comes cold and simple: this is how it happens, in a street you have walked a hundred times. After they run, he slides down the wall and stays there longer than he later admits. His body shakes so violently he cannot type his passcode when he tries to call for help.

In the first days after, he tells the story in a flat, efficient way. He gives a statement, replaces his bank cards, answers messages from worried colleagues. He says he is "fine," irritated by how often people ask. What he does not say is that sleep changes immediately. Each time he starts to drift off, he is back against the wall with a hand at his throat or hears footsteps approaching from behind. Sometimes the dreams match what happened; sometimes they are worse, with a knife that was never there. He wakes drenched in sweat, heart racing, and reaches for the bedside lamp before he is fully awake. His girlfriend begins to stir whenever he jerks upright. At first he apologizes. Later he starts sleeping lightly on purpose, as if vigilance might prevent the dreams.

He returns to work quickly because that is what he believes a capable person should do. On the water he still performs well enough, but something in him is less flexible. Sudden radio crackle makes him flinch. If a crew member comes up behind him unexpectedly, his shoulders lock and he spins around too fast, embarrassed by the force of it. He begins scanning everyone around the dock-hands, pockets, distance to exits-without deciding to. In the Coast Guard he has been trained to assess risk, and this habit gives his hypervigilance a convincing disguise. He tells himself he is just being observant. But he notices that his attention no longer settles. During briefings, parts of conversations drop away when a noise in the corridor catches him. Off shift, he chooses routes home with open sight lines and brighter lighting, even when they take twice as long.

His girlfriend first experiences the change as irritability. He snaps when she asks whether he is coming to bed, when she leaves the curtains half open, when she suggests meeting friends in town. Crowded pubs become intolerable. He stands with his back to the wall, drinking too quickly, pretending to listen while tracking every person who passes near their table. Once, when a stranger bumps his shoulder, his whole body surges with adrenaline and he has to leave before he does something he will regret. After that he starts declining invitations. He says he is tired, that work is busy, that he would rather stay in. The apartment becomes both refuge and trap. He checks the door repeatedly at night now, then checks the windows, then listens in the hallway for sounds that do not mean anything.

What unsettles him most is not fear alone but the collapse of his assumptions about himself. He is physically fit, trained, used to emergencies, and yet in his mind the robbery replays as a private failure. He thinks he should have seen them sooner, should have fought differently, should not have frozen. The memory intrudes while he is shaving, while he is tying ropes at work, while he is waiting for coffee to brew. Sometimes it is an image; sometimes it is the felt sense of being trapped. If he catches the smell of stale smoke on the street, his stomach drops before he understands why. He avoids the convenience store entirely. He avoids the street where it happened, then several surrounding blocks, then any errand that would bring him out after dark alone.

Months later, his world is narrower. He still goes to work, still puts on the uniform, still answers with "all good" when colleagues ask. But his girlfriend notices he no longer runs in the evening and no longer walks anywhere without turning to check behind him. He notices he cannot remember the last time he felt fully at ease. Even in his own home, even beside someone who loves him, part of him remains braced for footsteps in the dark.
